title: NASA Turns to Commercial Space Industry to Rescue Hubble Telescope, Says Verge Report
body:
NASA’s next big challenge may not be launching a new telescope but keeping the iconic Hubble Space Telescope aloft until a safe retirement. With its orbital lifetime running out in the early 2030s, the agency is looking to the burgeoning commercial space sector for a cost‑effective boost that could extend Hubble’s scientific service or at least shepherd it to a controlled re‑entry, officials said this week.

The aging observatory, launched in 1990, has delivered some of the most detailed images of the cosmos, from the Pillars of Creation to the first direct evidence of dark energy. Its orbit, however, is slowly decaying due to atmospheric drag at an altitude of roughly 540 km. Without a maneuver to raise it, Hubble will eventually plunge back into Earth’s atmosphere, burning up over a broad swath of the planet. NASA estimates that, without intervention, the telescope could re‑enter uncontrolled as early as 2034, posing a small but non‑zero risk of debris reaching the surface.

Historically, NASA has relied on its own shuttle fleet and, later, the European Space Agency’s (ESA) service missions to keep Hubble operational. The final servicing mission in 2009, executed by shuttle astronauts, upgraded the telescope’s gyroscopes, batteries, and instruments, extending its life by another decade. Since the retirement of the shuttle program, NASA’s ability to conduct on‑orbit repairs has been limited to robotic missions such as the 2021 “Hubble Legacy” proposal, which was ultimately deemed too costly and technically risky. The agency now sees a partnership with private launch providers as the most viable path forward.

Commercial firms have already demonstrated the capability to deliver payloads to low‑Earth orbit at a fraction of the cost of traditional government launches. Companies like SpaceX, United Launch Alliance (ULA), and Blue Origin operate reusable rockets that can carry several tons to the same altitude where Hubble resides. NASA’s Commercial Orbital Transportation Services (COTS) and Commercial Crew Programs have proven that the agency can effectively outsource routine logistics to the private sector. In the case of Hubble, a modestly sized propulsion module attached to the telescope could raise its orbit by a few dozen kilometers, buying an additional 5–10 years of observation time while also positioning it for a controlled de‑orbit at the end of its life.

Critics argue that the financial and engineering hurdles of attaching a new propulsion system to a 30‑year‑old spacecraft are significant. The telescope’s original design did not anticipate such retrofits, and any maneuver would require precise navigation to avoid contaminating its delicate optics. Moreover, the cost of a dedicated launch, even at commercial rates, could run into the hundreds of millions of dollars—funds that must compete with NASA’s other priorities, including the James Webb Space Telescope and the forthcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Nonetheless, proponents contend that the scientific return on extending Hubble’s mission, even modestly, justifies the expense, especially given the telescope’s unique ultraviolet capabilities that newer observatories lack.

The conversation also touches on broader policy questions about the role of commercial actors in legacy space infrastructure. If a private company can provide a “towing” service for Hubble, it could set a precedent for similar interventions with other aging satellites, potentially creating a new market for orbital maintenance and debris mitigation. Such a model would align with NASA’s long‑term strategy to outsource routine operations while focusing its own resources on deep‑space exploration and next‑generation science missions.

As the 2030s approach, NASA’s leadership plans to convene a working group that will assess technical feasibility, cost estimates, and risk mitigation strategies for a commercial boost or de‑orbit solution. The outcome will shape not only Hubble’s final chapter but also the evolving partnership between government and industry in safeguarding the orbital environment. Whether the telescope will glide gracefully into a planned re‑entry or enjoy a few more years of groundbreaking observations, the effort underscores a pivotal moment: the transition from a government‑centric era of space operations to a collaborative ecosystem where commercial ingenuity may preserve humanity’s most cherished windows to the universe.
